title: Anaphylaxis / Allergic Reaction
desc: Volumes worked out by severity — mild skin reaction, mild systemic, severe systemic and localised — for diphenhydramine, Dex SP, epinephrine, atropine and terbutaline.

meds.name: Epinephrine 1:1000
meds.note: 0.01 mg/kg. With 1:1000 (1 mg/ml) the millilitres equal the milligrams.

meds.name: Epinephrine 1:1000
meds.note: This is the drug that matters in severe anaphylaxis, and the one most often delayed. Repeat every 5 to 15 minutes as needed.

meds.name: Dex SP
meds.desc: higher dose than the mild protocol
meds.note: 0.5 to 1 mg/kg IV in severe cases. At 4 mg/ml, divide the milligrams above by 4 for the volume in ml.

meds.name: Epinephrine 1:1000 at the site
meds.doseText: 0.15 ml at the site of the injection

meds.name: Terbutaline
meds.note: Cats in anaphylaxis present with respiratory signs rather than the collapse seen in dogs — terbutaline is the feline-specific addition.

meds.name: Epinephrine 1:1000
meds.note: Repeat every 5 to 15 minutes as needed.

meds.name: Dex SP
meds.desc: higher dose than the mild protocol
meds.note: 0.5 to 1 mg/kg IV. At 4 mg/ml, divide by 4 for the volume in ml.

notes.Epinephrine first: In severe systemic anaphylaxis, epinephrine is the drug that changes the outcome. Antihistamines and steroids do not treat the acute event — give the epinephrine and do not wait to see whether the others work.
notes.Concentration: Epinephrine 1:1000 is 1 mg/ml, so the millilitres equal the milligrams at 0.01 mg/kg.
notes.Cats present differently: Cats show respiratory distress rather than the vascular collapse typical of dogs. Terbutaline 0.01 mg/kg is the feline-specific addition.
notes.Dexamethasone dose changes with severity: 0.25 mg/kg for mild reactions; 0.5 to 1 mg/kg IV for severe systemic anaphylaxis.
notes.Localised reactions: Diphenhydramine 2.2 mg/kg, Dex SP 0.25 mg/kg, and 0.15 ml of epinephrine 1:1000 infiltrated at the site of the injection.

dischargeBlocks.title: What happened today
dischargeBlocks.text:
{name} had an allergic reaction. We have treated it and the immediate danger has passed, but reactions can occasionally come back a few hours later.

Please keep {name} quiet and where you can see them for the rest of today and tonight.

dischargeBlocks.title: Come straight back, or go to an emergency hospital, if you see
dischargeBlocks.text:
- Swelling of the face, muzzle, eyes or throat
- Difficulty breathing, noisy breathing, or open-mouthed breathing
- Vomiting or diarrhea, especially with weakness
- Pale gums, collapse, or unsteadiness
- Widespread hives or intense itching returning

Do not wait to see whether it settles. A returning reaction can move quickly.

dischargeBlocks.title: What caused it
dischargeBlocks.text:
We often cannot identify the trigger with certainty. Common ones are insect stings, medications, vaccines and foods.

If you know what {name} was exposed to, please tell us so we can record it — that matters for future vaccinations, anaesthetics and prescriptions.

dischargeBlocks.title: Follow up
dischargeBlocks.text: Call us tomorrow to let us know how {name} is. If reactions have happened more than once we should talk about what to avoid, and whether you should keep anything at home.
